o: Explain the purpose of firewalls and anti-malware software.
Describe user access levels and security updates.
Choose controls appropriate to malware, interception or unauthorised access.
c: A vulnerability is a weakness that an attacker might exploit. Using multiple security measures reduces risk.
A firewall monitors/filters network traffic using rules, blocking or allowing connections according to security policy.
Anti-malware software detects and may remove malicious software. Software updates can fix known security weaknesses.
Access rights restrict what users can view or change, reducing the damage possible if a lower-privilege account is compromised.

m.title: Protect a school file server
m.q: Explain how a firewall and user access levels help protect a school file server. [4 marks]
st: The file server faces network traffic and has confidential resources.
A firewall filters incoming/outgoing network traffic [1], blocking connections that violate security rules [1].
User access levels limit permissions [1], preventing ordinary users from editing or viewing protected files [1].
Two distinct defences with their actions and security benefits.

w: A classroom PC may be infected by downloaded malware. Explain how anti-malware software and updates reduce risk. [4 marks]
Anti-malware scans for malicious code [1] and can quarantine/remove it [1]. Security updates patch known software weaknesses [1], making exploitation of those vulnerabilities less likely [1].
A school wants to limit access to staff records. Explain how access levels can help. [4 marks]

Permissions give access only to authorised accounts [1], restricting who can read records [1]. A normal student account has lower privileges [1], reducing the changes it can make to sensitive information [1].
A school firewall blocks an unfamiliar network connection. Explain what the firewall does and one limitation. [4 marks]
Firewall uses rules to check network traffic [1] and blocks disallowed connections [1]. It cannot guarantee stopping every threat [1], especially if a user runs malware already inside the device [1].

Access permissions restrict resources [1]; student accounts get fewer privileges [1].
Unauthorised records stay private and damage is limited [2].

Describe filtering, then explain why layered controls remain useful.
Traffic is examined against rules and blocked if disallowed [2].
Other types of compromise still need anti-malware or user training [2].
Firewall uses rules to check network traffic [1] and blocks disallowed connections [1]. It cannot guarantee stopping every threat [1], especially if a user runs malware already inside the device [1].

k.q: Model whether a firewall rule allows or blocks an already-classified connection.
k.code:
authorised = 0
if authorised > 0 then
    print("Allow connection")
else
    print("Block connection")
endif
k.a:
At 0: Block connection; at 1: Allow connection.

Extended OCR ERL:
authorised = 1
if authorised > 0 then
    print("Allow connection")
else
    print("Block connection")
endif
print("Rule checked")

Outputs: Allow connection; Rule checked. Real firewall rules are more involved.

Explain how anti-malware and user access levels protect shared school computers. [4 marks]

Source: Original OCR J277-style question, not a past-paper original.
Anti-malware detects/removes harmful software [2]. User access levels restrict permissions [1] and limit the files/settings that can be changed [1].

Explain how firewalls, updates and permissions combine to reduce security risks. [6 marks]

Source: Original OCR J277-style question, not a past-paper original.

Firewall filters traffic [1], blocking disallowed connections [1]. Updates repair software weaknesses [1], reducing opportunities for exploitation [1]. Access levels restrict users' permissions [1], limiting exposure or damage [1].

State one benefit of agreed networking standards. [1 mark]
They allow equipment/software from different manufacturers to communicate/interoperate [1].
Explain one difference between HTTP and HTTPS and why it matters for online payments. [4 marks]
HTTP transfers web content [1]; HTTPS encrypts the connection [1], so intercepted data is not readable without the correct key [1] and protects payment details in transit [1].
